title: Ask Jason which provider-auth mechanism Haven will use; the SAN rule binds only the PKIX path
description:
Found 2026-11-22 while verifying the mTLS proxy path on
mimi.reviewcommit.com (bead mimid-1wgh.46.20.1).

mimid refuses a peer client certificate that does not assert the
provider's domain in a dNSName subjectAltName. A Subject CN is not
accepted. The refusal is:

    request refused: provider not authenticated
    reason=certificate refused: no dNSName for the domain

This is correct behaviour -- CN-as-hostname is deprecated, and
draft-atwood-mimi-provider-auth-00 §7 is about the domain a certificate
asserts -- but it will fail interop silently if Haven's certificate
carries only a CN. Both sides would see a 403 with no hint about why.

ACTION: confirm with Jason before the interop day that Haven's client
certificate for its provider domain has a dNSName SAN for that domain.
Telling him needs Mark's OK, like any upstream contact.

Second, smaller finding from the same test: a client certificate must
use a signature algorithm the TLS CertificateRequest offers. An Ed25519
test certificate was silently not sent by curl/OpenSSL against Caddy;
ECDSA P-256 was sent. Ordinary RSA or ECDSA certificates are fine, but
if Haven uses Ed25519 the handshake will present no certificate at all
and mimid will report "no credentials" rather than anything about the
certificate -- a confusing failure worth knowing in advance.
notes:
CORRECTED 2026-11-22 after Mark asked whether needing this means our
spec is too strict. Checked the draft and RFC 9525. Answer: the spec is
NOT too strict, and my original framing of this bead overstated what
Haven has to do.

1. The dNSName requirement is RFC 9525 compliance, not our invention.
   draft-atwood-mimi-provider-auth-00 §7 (pkix) says: "The certificate
   MUST contain a subjectAltName dNSName that is the provider domain"
   and "It matches the provider domain against the certificate as a
   DNS-ID per [RFC9525]; it does not use the subject common name."
   RFC 9525 (2023), which obsoletes RFC 6125, REMOVES CN-ID: using a
   Subject CN as a reference identifier is forbidden, not merely
   discouraged. Accepting a CN would mean contradicting a current
   standards-track RFC and reintroducing a practice the IETF spent a
   decade removing. A dNSName SAN has also been mandatory in the Web PKI
   for over a decade, so this is not an unusual thing to ask of a
   certificate.

2. The requirement binds ONLY the optional mechanism. §7 is the
   "MAY present a client certificate" path for providers with an
   existing PKI. Haven has two other routes that do not need a SAN at
   all:
   - DANE-EE: "With the DANE-EE usage the certificate's names are not
     checked" (§6, citing RFC 7671 §5.1). A certificate with no SAN
     works.
   - RFC 9421 DNS keys, the primary mechanism: no certificate at all.
   So Haven is not obliged to change its certificate. It only matters if
   Haven chooses the PKIX-from-configured-anchors path.

3. WHAT IS ACTUALLY WORTH FIXING is diagnosability on the PKIX path, and
   that is on our side. A peer whose certificate is refused for a bad or
   missing SAN gets a bare 403 with
   type=...:problem:provider-authentication. The reason
   ("certificate refused: no dNSName for the domain") appears only in
   mimid's own debug log, so the peer cannot learn why. It does get a
   useful Accept-Signature header:
     mimi=("@method" "@target-uri" "content-digest" "from");created;tag="mimi";alg="ed25519"
   which correctly steers it to the signature mechanism -- but that
   means a PKIX misconfiguration is silently invisible and reads as
   "use signatures instead". Filed separately.

REVISED ACTION: do not ask Haven to change anything on this account.
Ask Jason only WHICH mechanism Haven intends for the interop day
(signatures, DANE, or PKIX), and mention the SAN requirement only if he
says PKIX. Contacting him still needs Mark's OK.

The Ed25519 observation stands and is unrelated to our spec: a client
certificate must use a signature algorithm the TLS CertificateRequest
offers, and an Ed25519 test certificate was silently not sent by
curl/OpenSSL against Caddy. That is a TLS-stack matter.
